config.why: About 120 g a day — and glycogen's 400–500 g is only about a day's reserve, which is why the tank runs out fast and surplus gets converted to fat.
config.context: liver and muscle hold roughly 400–500 g of glycogen — about one day

activities.anchor: one of the mechanisms behind "fat keeps you full"
activities.caption: drag between the two fuel tanks
activities.name: nutTanksCompare

config.prompt: Drag across the body's two energy stores:

before.label: glycogen — the quick shelf
before.text: About 400–500 g in liver and muscle, roughly 2,000 kcal in total: a day's reserve, gone quickly.

after.label: adipose — the deep tank
after.text: About 9,000 kcal per kilogram: the dense fuel at 9 kcal/g, the carrier for vitamins A, D, E and K, the raw material of hormones.

config.why: Two tanks of wildly different capacity — and emulsified by bile, hydrolysed by lipase, fat is also absorbed slowly enough to extend satiety.

activities.anchor: high folate can hide B12 deficiency while the nerve damage progresses
activities.caption: true or false — the dose makes the poison
activities.name: nutMegaJudge

statements.s: Vitamins are harmless because they are natural — more is always better.
statements.why: Fat-soluble vitamins are stored, and chronic megadoses of A or D cause documented organ damage.

statements.s: High-dose supplements can interfere with medications or mask other deficiencies.
statements.why: The folate–B12 case is the classic — the anaemia hides while nerve damage progresses.

statements.s: Deficiency is the only danger vitamins pose.
statements.why: Micronutrients run in windows — both ends of every nutrient curve are disease.

statements.s: Nutrients inside foods arrive with fibre, water and co-factors at doses the body evolved to handle.
statements.why: The contrast with concentrated pills — company matters chemically.

activities.anchor: sodium guards the outside while potassium guards the inside
activities.caption: place the marker — the body's water map
activities.name: nutWaterPlace

config.prompt: In a 70 kg adult holding about 42 L of water — how many litres sit inside cells?
config.why: About 28 L inside cells, 14 L outside (blood plasma plus interstitial fluid) — the gradients between them are the electrochemistry of nerve and muscle.

activities.anchor: an hour at the gym is water, not marketing
activities.caption: walk the over-drinking case
activities.name: nutSweatBranch

config.root: A marathon runner drinks only plain water through a six-hour summer race. Walk what can go wrong.

start.text: Sweat carries water and what else?

choices.label: Mostly water — dissolved salts hardly matter
Roughly a gram of sodium per litre

wrong.text: Sodium sets osmolarity, membrane voltage and fluid volume — sweat carries a real salt load with it.

sodium.text: Replacing water but not sodium can dilute the remaining body sodium — exercise-associated hyponatraemia, the documented cause of marathon deaths from over-drinking.

done.text: Electrolyte replacement matters in proportion to sweat volume and duration — an hour at the gym is one prescription, a six-hour shift another.

config.why: Water needs vary, food supplies about a fifth of typical fluid intake, and thirst is a workable guide in healthy people — the arithmetic beats the slogan.
